extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, typesetters, and publishers preparing multilingual and mathematical manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for transliteration, word division, and typographic treatment of languages other than English (Russian, Greek, South Asian, Old/Middle English, ASL) and for preparing and editing mathematical expressions for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian word-division: consonant division
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be divided between single consonants or between a consonant and a consonant combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ubor-ku, chudes-nym, mol-cha. Observe how single consonants or consonant+combination are treated when hyphenating at line breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian word-division: undivided consonant clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain consonant combinations are not normally divided when breaking words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List (original wording): bl, br, dr, dv, fl, fr, gl, gr, kl, kr, ml, pl, pr, sk, skr, skv, st, str, stv, tr, tv, vl, vr, zhd. They may be divided if they fall across a boundary of a prefix and a root or other morphological units (e.g., ob-lech’, ras-kol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian word-division: division after prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be divided after a prefix, but generally the prefix itself should not be divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bes-poryadok, pere-stroyka, za-dat’, pred-lozhit’, pro-vesti, obo-gnat’. Editors should avoid splitting the prefix unless morphological boundary requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian word-division: compounds divided between parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words should be divided between parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: radio-priyémnik, gor-sovet, kino-teatr. When hyphenating compounds, split at the part boundary rather than within morphemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russian word-division: division after vowel or diphthong
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be divided after a vowel or a diphthong before a single (Cyrillic) consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Si-bir’, voy-na, Gorba-chev, da-zhe. Division after a vowel may also be made before a consonant combination: puteshe-stvennik, khi-trit’, pro-stak, ru-brika.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Asian transliteration: diacritic usage and simplified practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Transliteration of South Asian languages may require special characters/diacritics, but many writers use a simplified style that omits diacritics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table shows special characters (Aa, Dd, Eé, Hh, Ii, LI, etc.). Note common simplifications: substituting 'sh' for various s’s, ignoring subscript dots for dental consonants, omitting macrons. Editors should be aware of both fully diacritic and simplified conventions and accept author preference unless publication standard differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek transliteration: omit accents and mark long vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated Greek words and phrases in works not focusing on ancient Greece are usually transliterated; in transliteration all Greek accents are omitted and macrons distinguish long vowels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use macron to distinguish eta and omega (long) from epsilon and omicron (short). Iota subscript transliterated on the line following the vowel; rough breathing transliterated by 'h' (precedes vowel/diphthong and follows r); smooth breathing ignored. If a diaeresis appears in Greek, preserve it in transliteration. Transliterated Greek words are usually italicized unless frequent (then italicize first mention only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting Greek: fonts and sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should use a Unicode-enabled font for Greek; publishers must ensure a Greek font is available and may need to adjust size to visually match surrounding type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek is normally not set in italics. Extra white space may be required where more than one diacritic appears over a vowel. Publishers should confirm font availability for publication and embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek breathings: marking and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: When Greek is set in the Greek alphabet, every initial vowel or diphthong or rho must be marked with a breathing (rough or smooth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breathing mark placed over lowercase initial vowel (or second vowel of diphthong) and positioned to the left of capital letters. A single quotation mark cannot substitute for a breathing mark because of size and positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek accents: types and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek has three accent marks (acute/oxia, circumflex/perispomeni, grave/varia) that occur only over vowels with placement rules tied to syllable position and capitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumflex occurs only on the two final syllables of a word; grave only on the last syllable. Like breathings, accents are placed over lowercase vowels, over the second vowel of a diphthong, and to the left of capital vowels. A diaeresis indicates that two successive vowels do not form a diphthong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek unaccented words: proclitics and enclitics exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most Greek words carry accents with two exceptions: proclitics and enclitics, which affect accent behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proclitics (certain articles, prepositions, conjunctions, adverb forms) are closely connected to following words and often unaccented. Enclitics are pronounced as part of the preceding word and usually lose their accents; in some circumstances the preceding word gains a second accent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek fonts must provide full diacritic coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Vowels with breathings and accents in all combinations are integral to every Greek font used in publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each font should supply all necessary combinations for lowercase and uppercase vowels; for scholarly work on manuscripts, additional symbols may be needed. Consult Unicode charts for up-to-date coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek punctuation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek punctuation differs from English in several marks and conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Period and comma same as English; colon and semicolon both a midlevel dot; question mark is a semicolon. The apostrophe (resembles a smooth breathing) is used as an elision mark. In English texts, quoted words or passages in the Greek alphabet should not be enclosed in quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek numerals: letters with numeral signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek numbers (when not written out) are represented by letters of the alphabet supplemented by obsolete letters and distinguished by diacritical numeral signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Greek numeral sign (U+0374) to mark numerals and Greek lower numeral sign (U+0375) for thousands. Publishers/typesetters should follow table 11.5 conventions for mapping letters to numeric values and for forming compound numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek word-division: diphthongs and vowel sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Diphthongs are never divided; two consecutive vowels that do not form a diphthong are divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rule contrasted: diphthongs (ai, av, etc.) remain intact; other vowel sequences split (Ge-d-o-pat). Apply phonological knowledge when hyphenating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek word-division: single consonant between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single consonant occurs between two vowels, divide the word before the consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pw-vt}, Ke-a-Aic, é-ya. Place hyphen so consonant begins the following syllable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek word-division: consonant clusters
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for dividing words with two or more consonants depend on cluster type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If consonant is doubled, or a mute is followed by its corresponding aspirate (e.g., nq, Bq, KX...), divide after the first consonant. If the cluster begins with a liquid (l, r) or a nasal (m, n), divide after the liquid or nasal. For other clusters, follow the general division (i.e., divide according to phonotactics within parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek compounds: divide between parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are divided between parts; within each part apply the usual hyphenation rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most compounds begin with a preposition or prefix—split at morphological boundary (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Old & Middle English: use correct special characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Special letters (edh, thorn, yogh, ligatures) that occur in Old/Middle English should be used in correct Unicode forms and supplied to the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide publisher with a list of special characters. Do not print certain ligatures as two letters in names and text (e.g., 4lfric). Use modern substitutions only where acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old & Middle English: ampersand/wynn and vowel marking
rubrics_metrics.description: Tironian et may appear historically, but modern ampersand may substitute; wynn may be replaced with modern w; long and short vowels sometimes distinguished by macrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modern ampersand when appropriate; mark long vowels with macron for editorial clarity; diphthongs usually marked with macron over the first vowel (except 2 ligature).

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL: signed-language components
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs have five major articulatory components: handshape, location, orientation, movement, and (in some cases) distinctive nonmanual signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcription and analysis should account for all five components when describing or notating signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL glosses: format and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The written-language transcription of a sign (gloss) uses small capital letters or regular capitals; when two or more written words gloss a single sign, separate with hyphens; translations are enclosed in double quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: WOMAN, SCHOOL, CAT; VEHICLE-DRIVE-BY is gloss for 'a car drove by.' Choose a consistent convention (small caps vs caps) and apply throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL compound signs: typographic indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound signs that have meanings separate from their parts can be indicated typographically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions include close-up marks or a plus sign. Examples: MOTHER FATHER or MOTHER+FATHER for 'parents.' Follow the transcription system's standard for compound marking.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL fingerspelling transcription conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fingerspelled words may be transcribed in various ways to indicate manual letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepted forms include fs-JOHN, J-O-H-N-, or j-o-h-n. Choose one consistent scheme; use 'fs-' prefix for explicit fingerspelling when desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL lexicalized signs: pound symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexicalized (commonly fingerspelled-turned-sign) forms are represented by the pound symbol '#'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: #WHAT, #BACK, #DO. Use '#' to mark lexicalized fingerspelled items.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL handshape labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Most ASL handshapes are described by corresponding alphabetic or numerical handshape names or idiosyncratic labels where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: APPLE = X handshape; CREATE = 4 handshape; SARCASTIC = HORNS handshape. For languages without the American Manual Alphabet, describe in relation to ASL handshapes if useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL sentence transcription: sequencing, punctuation, and translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Signed sentences are written as a sequence of glosses, often with the spoken/written-language translation underneath in italics or quotes; punctuation is generally omitted from the transcription though translations keep punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some writers add question marks or exclamation points in glosses and commas to indicate short pauses. Maintain consistent alignment between gloss and translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL pronouns/possessives/coreference indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns commonly glossed as IX or PRO followed by person/number indicators; possessives glossed as Poss; subscript indices show co-reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conventions vary (IX3p, IX-3p, PRO.3). Use subscript indices to indicate that different signs/coreferential noun phrases refer to the same referent. Example alignment: IX3pi LOSE POSS3pi HOUSE -> 'He lost his house.'

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL nonmanual signals: labeling and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonmanual gestures (facial expressions, etc.) are labeled (e.g., whq for question facial expression) and typeset in a smaller font with a half-point rule above the ASL sentence; correct alignment with manual signs is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonmanual labels indicate grammatical functions and are extended over the manual signs they accompany; ensure alignment to reflect simultaneity (e.g., whq occurring over entire question).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics in type: author/editor attention to clarity and field conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and editors should attend to style, usage, sense, meaning, clarity, accuracy, and consistency; follow the conventions of the author's special field while querying apparent typographical or grammatical violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most cases the author's preferences should prevail; mathematical copy should read as clearly and grammatically as prose. Editors should not unilaterally change mathematical notation without consulting the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics: recommended tools and markup awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Use LaTeX for extensive mathematical work; editors should understand LaTeX markup to avoid unnecessary changes. Occasional math can be done with word-processor equation editors; MathML is relevant for electronic publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should know when changes can be global in LaTeX. Authors should consult MathML standards for web/electronic accessibility and prepare paper manuscripts according to specified marking guidelines (see 12.61-68).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical notation: consistency of symbols and typographical distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and symbols should be used consistently and unambiguously; the same symbol should denote the same thing and not be reused for different objects without good reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make consistent use of typographical distinctions (italic, roman, bold) for different mathematical objects (e.g., sets vs elements). Avoid introducing symbols that appear only once unless later qualified; editors should not delete symbols without author instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words versus symbols in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical symbols may appear in text, but logical symbols and awkward symbol shorthands should generally be written out in words for grammatical clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer textual rendering for logical connectives (e.g., 'there exists' rather than the symbol ∃) and avoid starting sentences with a symbol; if unavoidable, supply the term in apposition or restructure the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical spacing: rules for binary ops/relations and subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary operation and relation signs are preceded and followed by medium spaces (about one-fourth em); no space when such signs modify a symbol (used adjectivally); in subscripts/superscripts no spaces around operation/relation signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: x + y has medium spaces; -1 or x5 (modifiers) have no spaces; in subscripts x_{a+b} avoid extra spacing. Proper spacing aids grouping and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical characters and fonts: availability and list preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Special mathematical characters and fonts may not be available in all typefaces; prepare a list of unusual mathematical signs and nonstandard fonts used in a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author should provide list to publisher; if characters are unavailable, the author may be asked to use accessible forms or the typesetter must obtain/generate needed characters. Prefer math-specific characters (not visually similar generic characters) because of intersymbol spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diacritics and special marks in math
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate diacritics (including stacked/over/under marks); when i or j carry diacritics, use dotless forms; double diacritics and grouped diacritics are allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure fonts support required diacritic combinations; maintain consistency in diacritic usage and prefer available Unicode/mathematical forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic letters and kerning in math
rubrics_metrics.description: Contiguous italic letters that represent separate mathematical objects must never be kerned; abbreviations formed from contiguous letters should be set roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fonts for mathematics are designed with reduced slant to avoid crowding. For example, 'Aut' (abbreviation) should be roman, not slanted and kerned as separate italic variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved meanings for special symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Many symbols have reserved or standard meanings (e.g., π, e, i; N, Z, Q, R, C for number systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use double-struck (blackboard) symbols for standard number sets (N, Z, Q, R, C). Avoid reassigning these symbols to unrelated objects without clear justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard abbreviated notations and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard abbreviations for functions (sin, cos, log, max, etc.) followed by a thin space unless the argument is in delimiters; limits are typeset as subscripts in text and below in display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sin x (thin space), sin(x+y) (no thin space before parenthesis). Use consistent conventions as in table 12.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation with mathematical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical expressions are grammatically part of the text and require correct sentence punctuation; displays that end sentences should carry ending punctuation; multiline consecutive lines of a single expression should not be punctuated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align ending punctuation and commas/semicolons horizontally on the baseline even when preceded by subscripts/superscripts/fractions. In elided lists, put commas after each term and after ellipsis if the list has a final term; place ellipsis on baseline when terms separated by commas, and choose baseline vs centered ellipsis position depending on whether operations/relations are elided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elided operations and relations: ellipsis placement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In elided sums or relations, the ellipsis should be vertically centered between operation or relation signs; for products, use baseline or centered ellipses depending on presence/absence of multiplication dot/cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for x1 + x2 + ... + xn use centered or baseline per surrounding notation; if multiplication dot present, ellipsis on baseline; if multiplication cross present, ellipsis centered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication notation: juxtaposition and explicit signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplication is often signified by juxtaposition (abc means a·b·c); when factors need separation, use explicit multiplication symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit signs (× or ·) where ambiguity may arise (e.g., 1×2, x·y vs x y). For numbers, choice between × and · can be stylistic but respect context (vectors use different signs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Displayed mathematics: when and how to display
rubrics_metrics.description: Display (set on separate line) mathematical expressions when they are important, referenced, or hard to read inline; separate multiple expressions on same line with spacing, words, or punctuation; align displays for readability (center or align on relation signs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center-align consecutive short displays or align on equals for groups of related equations. Qualifying clauses may be displayed as well and separated from the main expression by an em space or more.
